full_citation: Kuo, T.-C., Kuo, C.-Y., and Chen, L.-W. (2022). Assessing environmental impacts of nanoscale semi-conductor manufacturing from the life cycle assessment perspective. Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 182, 106289.
peer_review_evidence: Full-length research article published in Resources, Conservation & Recycling; manuscript records acceptance on 10 March 2022. Journal peer-review policy was not separately documented in this review.
research_objective: Assess life-cycle impacts of a memory-manufacturer case and compare environmental impact across 20 nm, 30 nm, and 40 nm technology nodes during 2018-2020.
semiconductor_feature: Embedded nonvolatile memory (eNVM) die fabrication; diffusion, photolithography, thin-film deposition, etching, and chemical-mechanical polishing; technology node and mask-layer effects.
data_or_variables: Inventory included electricity, diesel, natural gas, tap water, process gases, chemicals, auxiliary materials, and waste outputs. Functional unit: a die for a technology node and mask layer. LCA used factory data from two factories and SimaPro 9.0 with ReCiPe 2016 (GWP100; IPCC2007).
environmental_impact: Climate change, water use, particulate matter, and mineral/metal resource use.
main_findings: Results report lower impacts for the 20 nm case than 30 nm and 40 nm; electricity use during manufacturing and wafer use were identified as major contributors. The article reports year-on-year reductions from 2018 to 2020, but some percentage text in the paper is internally unclear, so no precise percentage is repeated here.
limitations: Single confidential memory-manufacturer case; inventory data came from two factories; results are specific to the selected product, technology nodes, mask layers, allocation, and system boundary. DRAM production was assessed cradle-to-grave, outsourced testing was excluded, and packaging data were identified as future work. The paper also notes uncertainty in inventory/model parameters.
dashboard_relevance: Supports showing that process node and mask-layer/product definition affect LCA results, and that electricity, water, and material inputs must be shown with functional unit and lifecycle boundary. It does not justify generalizing its case results to all manufacturers.
review_status: Full text reviewed (9-page PDF); objective, functional unit, inventory, LCA method, findings, and limitations checked. Peer-review process not independently verified.

full_citation: Ruberti, M. (2024). Environmental performance and trends of the world's semiconductor foundry industry. Journal of Industrial Ecology, 28(5), 1183-1197.
peer_review_evidence: Open-access research article in Journal of Industrial Ecology, published 16 July 2024; publisher labels it a research article. Peer-review process was not independently documented in the reviewed PDF.
research_objective: Assess environmental performance and historical trends of the global semiconductor foundry industry from 2012 to 2021 using company-report disclosures and common production-normalized indicators.
semiconductor_feature: Leading semiconductor foundries; the company sample represents about 70% of global foundry revenue. Six foundries are compared in the study's common-index analyses.
data_or_variables: CSR reports plus company, industry, and public-source data; production, revenue, R&D, patents, Scope 1/2 GHG emissions, energy, water, wastewater, general and hazardous waste; KPIs normalized using a common manufacturing index (MI). The MI conversion estimates wafer area and assumes about 30 mask layers per wafer.
environmental_impact: Energy and water use; Scope 1/2 GHG emissions; wastewater; general and hazardous waste; absolute and manufacturing-index-normalized trends.
main_findings: From 2012 to 2021, patents, wafer production, and revenue rose 400%, 183%, and 172%, respectively. Absolute energy use rose 164%, water use 163%, general waste 568%, and hazardous waste 239%. Per MI, energy and water were broadly stable, hazardous waste increased 20%, and Scope 1/2 GHG emissions declined 32%, mainly attributed to renewable-energy investment.
limitations: Based on company disclosures with known readability/transparency and comparability limits; the sample is not the entire value chain or every foundry. KPI availability determines what can be compared. F-GHG emissions were omitted where data were unavailable; Scope 3 reporting was incomplete. Common MI normalization requires assumptions (including approximately 30 mask layers) and should not be treated as a universal production standard. Data supporting findings are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request; no formal uncertainty/sensitivity analysis was identified in the reviewed sections.
dashboard_relevance: Supports historical trend and intensity views alongside absolute totals, explicit disclosure coverage, and production-normalization assumptions. Demonstrates that absolute growth may coexist with stable intensity or declining Scope 1/2 emissions per MI; do not conflate these outcomes.
review_status: Full text reviewed from rendered PDF pages (34-page image-only copy); article identity/abstract, CSR-report method, common-MI assumptions, 2012-2021 results, conclusions, and data/reporting limitations checked. Publisher identifies it as an open-access research article; peer-review process not separately verified.

full_citation: Wang, Q., Huang, N., Chen, Z., Chen, X., Cai, H., and Wu, Y. (2023). Environmental data and facts in the semiconductor manufacturing industry: An unexpected high water and energy consumption situation. Water Cycle, 4, 47-54.
peer_review_evidence: Full-text research article published in Water Cycle; article declares funding and no known competing interests. Journal peer-review process was not independently verified.
research_objective: Survey environmental stewardship information and aggregate water, energy, and GHG data for semiconductor corporations.
semiconductor_feature: Semiconductor manufacturing corporations in multiple countries/regions; 28 corporations selected based on published industry information.
data_or_variables: 2021 or recent CSR/ESG reports; water withdrawal by source; energy consumption and source; Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions; UPW use; production-normalized indicators where reported.
environmental_impact: Water withdrawal and sources; ultrapure-water use; energy consumption and mix; direct and indirect GHG emissions.
main_findings: The authors report 2021 totals of 7.89 × 10^8 m3 water withdrawal and 1.49 × 10^11 kWh energy use for 27 corporations, and 7.15 × 10^7 t CO2e GHG emissions for 26 corporations. Scope 1 and 2 account for 2.74 × 10^7 and 4.41 × 10^7 t CO2e. Nine corporations reported UPW use; the six-company product-normalized series is based on announced company data.
limitations: Compiled from CSR/ESG disclosures for 2021 or recent years, with TSEM represented by an earlier report. Water/energy totals include 27 corporations and GHG includes 26 because YMTC did not disclose GHG data. Reporting availability and denominators therefore vary; product-normalized metrics are not reported for all companies. Treat results as disclosure-derived aggregates, not independently measured or fully harmonized observations; the article does not present a formal uncertainty/sensitivity analysis in the reviewed text.
dashboard_relevance: Useful for contextualizing water, energy, water-source, UPW, and Scope 1/2 indicators, and for warning that coverage and denominators must accompany aggregates. Its totals are not directly comparable to the project's heterogeneous observations and are not imported into the dataset.
review_status: Full text reviewed (8-page PDF); disclosure-based method, denominators, reported totals, UPW discussion, and study limitations checked. Peer-review process not independently verified.

full_citation: Ruberti, M. (2023). The chip manufacturing industry: Environmental impacts and eco-efficiency analysis. Science of the Total Environment, 858, 159873.
peer_review_evidence: Full-length research article published in Science of the Total Environment; accepted 27 October 2022 and published online 2 November 2022. Journal peer-review policy was not separately documented in this review.
research_objective: Compare environmental performance and eco-efficiency among leading semiconductor foundries, examining how company scale and technological capacity relate to impact.
semiconductor_feature: Six foundries/fabs: TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries (GF), SMIC, PSMC, and HHS.
data_or_variables: CSR-report data for revenue, R&D expenses, production, Scope 1/2 and fluorinated GHG, energy, water withdrawal, wastewater, and general/hazardous waste. Heterogeneous production units were converted to a common manufacturing index based on wafer area and an assumed 45 mask layers.
environmental_impact: Energy and water intensity, wastewater, Scope 1/2 and fluorinated GHG emissions, general and hazardous waste; eco-efficiency indicators normalized to manufacturing index.
main_findings: The normalized comparisons indicate that greater company size, revenue per production unit, and technological capacity do not consistently correspond to lower per-unit energy, water, waste, wastewater, or GHG impact. Scope 2 emissions were generally higher than Scope 1 in the compared data.
limitations: CSR-report availability constrained metric selection and comparability. The common manufacturing index depends on simplifying assumptions (including 45 mask layers); only TSMC and UMC reported Scope 3, so Scope 3 was excluded. Metrics are disclosure-derived and the six-fab sample is not a census or independently harmonized facility inventory.
dashboard_relevance: Supports displaying production-normalized environmental metrics with explicit definitions and cautioning against assumptions that scale or advanced nodes automatically imply lower impact. Do not treat the article's index as a standardized universal unit.
review_status: Full text reviewed (11-page PDF); six-company scope, source data, manufacturing-index method, key findings, Scope 3 exclusion, data-availability constraints, and disclosures checked.

full_citation: Frost, K., & Hua, I. (2019). Quantifying spatiotemporal impacts of the interaction of water scarcity and water use by the global semiconductor manufacturing industry. Water Resources and Industry, 22, 100115.
peer_review_evidence: Full-length open-access research article published in Water Resources and Industry; publication metadata and article details checked in uploaded PDF. Peer-review process was not separately documented in this review.
research_objective: Estimate the geographic and seasonal distribution of semiconductor manufacturing water withdrawals and identify locations where withdrawals interact with water scarcity.
semiconductor_feature: Global semiconductor fabrication facilities and production lines; direct fab feedwater and indirect electricity-related water withdrawals.
data_or_variables: Bottom-up estimates using Q4 2016 production data; methods report 1,021 valid production-line records and results describe 1,020 analyzed facilities/lines. Inputs include technology-specific chip/wafer water and electricity intensities, facility geolocation, regional electricity water-use intensity factors, and AWaRe scarcity factors for 202 watersheds.
environmental_impact: Direct feedwater (FW/Scope 1) and electricity-related water (ERW/Scope 2) withdrawals; scarcity-weighted FW withdrawals in liters of H2O equivalents; annual and seasonal watershed variation.
main_findings: The modeled inventory covers nearly all semiconductor manufacturing capacity in Q4 2016. Electricity-related withdrawals dominate in many settings (reported as 10-50 times direct withdrawals in some cases). About 47% of production was in areas with above-global-average scarcity and almost 13% in very water-scarce areas. AWaRe weighting was applied to direct feedwater in 202 watersheds.
limitations: Model estimates rely on technology/production assumptions and regional electricity water-use factors; the PDF gives slightly different counts (1,021 valid production-line records in methods versus 1,020 analyzed facilities/lines in results). Some facilities may operate below assumed capacity. Withdrawals are a conservative proxy rather than consumptive use and do not account for recycling/returns or water quality. The analysis excludes electricity-related water from chip use-phase and does not fully benchmark modeled facility estimates against observed facility data. Scarcity-weighted withdrawals are screening indicators, not direct measurements of physical scarcity or manufacturer operational risk.
dashboard_relevance: Supports separating direct and electricity-related water, attaching location/time context to water indicators, and labeling modeled/scarcity-weighted values distinctly from company-reported withdrawals.
review_status: Full text reviewed (21-page PDF); system boundary, production-data coverage and its internal count discrepancy, modeled inputs, FW/ERW distinction, AWaRe method, results, and explicit limitations checked.
